name: The discharged soldier's house at the forks, 1812
aka: 'two houses at the forks, one occupied by a discharged soldier' (Quaife 1913, reading Whistler's draught)

grade.why: Placed by our reconstruction of the town; no source pictures or records it here.

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS INFERRED FROM TWO WITNESSES OF 1808 AND A BOUND THIS PROJECT CHOSE. It opens on 25 January 1808, the date Whistler's draught carries, the one day a source shows the house standing; Surgeon Cooper, at the post from 1808, counts one house near the forks, which this project takes to be the draught's other house (forks_house_clark_1812) (Quaife 1913 p. 167). It may be older. No source read for T-2512 mentions it after Cooper's years, so its standing on the scene date of August 1812 is inferred from continuity, as the La Lime house's is. It is closed on 3 July 1816, the day before the troops came back to rebuild the fort: nothing read names a house at the forks in any account of the reoccupied post, and the close keeps it out of every scene after 1812 rather than carrying an unwitnessed house into one. The close is reconstructed (L-1812-forks-2512).

change_note: Built T-2512 (2026-10-15), one of the two houses Whistler's 1808 draught draws at the forks of the river, in the 1812 scene.

placement.position_note: Whistler's draught of 25 January 1808 draws two small houses at the bottom left of the sheet, where the double line of the river (index no. 25) meets a second double line lettered 'One branch of Cheykago River': one in the angle between the branch and the river, across the river from the fort, and one on the fort's side of the river beside the dotted outline lettered 'Company Garden & public Cornfield Eight acres'. Quaife (1913 p. 167): 'Whistler's drawing represents two houses at the forks, one occupied by a discharged soldier.' The committed trace's 34-item index does not number them; they were found on the pinned sheet at T-2512. THE RULING: the draught's 'One branch' is the North Branch, because the river line it meets is the main stem coming round from the fort and the cornfield Quaife puts 'on the south side of the main river' is drawn on the fort's side of that line; so this house, drawn across the main stem from the fort and on the near side of the branch, stands on the north bank east of the North Branch. On the committed forks water (Wright 1834, +/-20 m) it is seated about 75 m east of the North Branch's east bank and 50 m north of the main stem's north bank, far enough that the bank's own uncertainty cannot put it in the water. The sheet's distances here are not to any scale, so nothing nearer is claimed. Rotation 0 is a reconstruction (L-1812-forks-2512).
placement.symbolic_location: On the north bank of the main river at the forks, in the angle between it and the North Branch, about 80 m east of the North Branch and 50 m north of the main stem. Local E +37.4..+42.7, N +52.1..+57.9.

footprint.note: THE DRAWN BOX AT THE INDEX'S FORTY FEET TO THE INCH, the scale the draught states for the Indian Department's dwellings and the one T-2062 reads every outside building at: sheet px [423, 1887, 462, 1930] (about +/-5 px) at 90.4 px to the inch is 17.3 x 19.0 ft. The drawing is a small pictorial elevation, roof and front together, so this is an upper bound (L-1812-forks-2512).

stories.note: Unattested. The draught draws a one-storey house; one storey with the roof space over it.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. About eight feet of log to the plate.

construction.note: No source states the material. Log is the bounded reading: every house at the post before 1812 whose material the histories give is log, and Quaife calls the factor's and the agent's houses 'two log houses' (L-1812-forks-2512).

roof_type.note: The draught draws a pitched roof over the house, as it does for the agent's house and the factory; a gable is the reading this project takes for all of them.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Unattested; no source describes the roof.

chimneys.note: Unattested. One end chimney, the least a winter house needs; no source places it.

function.note: A dwelling. Quaife, reading Whistler's draught: 'one occupied by a discharged soldier'. Which of the two forks houses the soldier lived in is a reconstruction (L-1812-forks-2512).

citations.citation: Quaife, Milo Milton. Chicago and the Old Northwest, 1673-1835: A Study of the Evolution of the Northwestern Frontier, together with a History of Fort Dearborn. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1913.

research_note: THE DISCHARGED SOLDIER'S HOUSE AT THE FORKS (T-2512). Whistler's draught of January 1808 draws two houses at the forks of the Chicago River, about two-thirds of a mile up the main stem from the fort, and Quaife says one was a discharged soldier's; the soldier is not named. WHICH HOUSE IS WHOSE IS NOT READ. Cooper, at the post from 1808, counts 'one near the forks of the river occupied by a man named Clark who was a cattle dealer' (Quaife 1913 p. 167); Whistler, the same winter, draws two at the forks and Quaife says one was a discharged soldier's. THE RULING: Clark's is the other of Whistler's two, so the forks have two houses and not three. Cooper's count of the houses round the post names one at the forks where Whistler draws two, and nothing read puts a third there; merging the cattle dealer into the draught's second house is the reading that adds no house a source does not draw. Which of the two drawn houses was Clark's and which the soldier's is not on the sheet as read: the lettering beside the western house is legible only as '... by the man of the House'. So this one is given to the soldier and the house on the south bank to Clark, and the choice is reconstructed. Everything of its shape is the archetype's small log house at the draught's drawn size (an upper bound); its seat is a ruling on the committed forks water. Nobody is drawn in or near it (L1).
